title: Pivot and unpivot
summary_md: Turn rows into columns with conditional aggregation (portable) or SQL Server PIVOT, turn columns back into rows, and know why dynamic columns need generated SQL.

sections.heading: Conditional aggregation pivot (works everywhere)
sections.body_md:
- **Rows to columns**: one output column per category value, each a `SUM(CASE WHEN category = 'x' THEN value END)`.
- `GROUP BY` the row key (here the date); the CASE routes each source row to its column.
- `ELSE 0` vs no ELSE is a choice: **0** says 'no sales', **NULL** says 'no data'. Without ELSE the sum of nothing is NULL.
- Works in MySQL, SQL Server and every other engine; the column list is fixed in the SQL text.

syntax.mysql:
SELECT key,
       SUM(CASE WHEN cat = 'A' THEN val ELSE 0 END) AS a,
       SUM(CASE WHEN cat = 'B' THEN val ELSE 0 END) AS b
FROM t
GROUP BY key;
syntax.tsql:
SELECT key,
       SUM(CASE WHEN cat = 'A' THEN val ELSE 0 END) AS a,
       SUM(CASE WHEN cat = 'B' THEN val ELSE 0 END) AS b
FROM t
GROUP BY key;

args.name: key
args.meaning: The row identity of the result (what you GROUP BY).

args.name: cat = 'A'
args.meaning: Which source rows feed this output column.

examples.title: Revenue per date, one column per region
examples.explain_md: East and West become columns. West has no row on 03-04, so `ELSE 0` yields 0 there.
examples.mysql:
SELECT sale_date,
       SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'East' THEN revenue ELSE 0 END) AS east,
       SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'West' THEN revenue ELSE 0 END) AS west
FROM daily_sales
WHERE sale_date <= '2024-03-05'
GROUP BY sale_date
ORDER BY sale_date;
examples.tsql:
SELECT sale_date,
       SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'East' THEN revenue ELSE 0 END) AS east,
       SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'West' THEN revenue ELSE 0 END) AS west
FROM daily_sales
WHERE sale_date <= '2024-03-05'
GROUP BY sale_date
ORDER BY sale_date;

examples.title: Same pivot with NULL for missing
examples.explain_md: Dropping `ELSE 0` makes the missing West day (03-04) NULL, which keeps 'no data' distinct from 'zero revenue'.
examples.mysql:
SELECT sale_date,
       SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'East' THEN revenue END) AS east,
       SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'West' THEN revenue END) AS west
FROM daily_sales
WHERE sale_date <= '2024-03-05'
GROUP BY sale_date
ORDER BY sale_date;
examples.tsql:
SELECT sale_date,
       SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'East' THEN revenue END) AS east,
       SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'West' THEN revenue END) AS west
FROM daily_sales
WHERE sale_date <= '2024-03-05'
GROUP BY sale_date
ORDER BY sale_date;

examples.title: Month x year comparison
examples.explain_md: Months become rows and each year becomes a column: a compact year-over-year table.
examples.mysql:
SELECT MONTH(month_start) AS month_num,
       SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(month_start) = 2023 THEN revenue END) AS rev_2023,
       SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(month_start) = 2024 THEN revenue END) AS rev_2024
FROM monthly_revenue
WHERE MONTH(month_start) <= 6
GROUP BY MONTH(month_start)
ORDER BY month_num;
examples.tsql:
SELECT MONTH(month_start) AS month_num,
       SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(month_start) = 2023 THEN revenue END) AS rev_2023,
       SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(month_start) = 2024 THEN revenue END) AS rev_2024
FROM monthly_revenue
WHERE MONTH(month_start) <= 6
GROUP BY MONTH(month_start)
ORDER BY month_num;

pitfalls_md: Selecting a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated breaks `ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY` (MySQL) and errors outright in SQL Server.

sections.heading: Variants: COUNT, MAX and shares
sections.body_md:
- **Counts**: `COUNT(CASE WHEN x THEN 1 END)` (COUNT skips the NULLs the CASE yields) or `SUM(CASE WHEN x THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.
- **Text or dates** in cells: use `MAX(CASE ...)` (or `MIN`): SUM does not work on strings, and MAX picks the one value when there is exactly one per cell.
- **Shares**: divide one conditional sum by the total.
- MySQL-only shorthand: `SUM(status = 'completed')` (booleans are 0/1). Not valid in SQL Server.

examples.title: Event counts per user
examples.explain_md: One row per user, one column per event type.
examples.mysql:
SELECT user_id,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN event_type = 'view' THEN 1 END) AS views,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN event_type = 'add_to_cart' THEN 1 END) AS carts,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN event_type = 'purchase' THEN 1 END) AS purchases
FROM events
GROUP BY user_id
ORDER BY user_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT user_id,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN event_type = 'view' THEN 1 END) AS views,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN event_type = 'add_to_cart' THEN 1 END) AS carts,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN event_type = 'purchase' THEN 1 END) AS purchases
FROM events
GROUP BY user_id
ORDER BY user_id;

examples.title: Order value by status per customer
examples.explain_md: Three amount columns per customer plus a grand total, from a single scan.
examples.mysql:
SELECT customer_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'completed' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS completed,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'refunded'  THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS refunded,
       SUM(amount) AS all_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT customer_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'completed' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS completed,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'refunded'  THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS refunded,
       SUM(amount) AS all_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;

examples.title: MAX(CASE ...) for non-additive values
examples.explain_md: Latest timestamp per event type per user; NULL where the user never did that action.
examples.mysql:
SELECT user_id,
       MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'view' THEN event_ts END) AS last_view,
       MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'purchase' THEN event_ts END) AS last_purchase
FROM events
GROUP BY user_id
ORDER BY user_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT user_id,
       MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'view' THEN event_ts END) AS last_view,
       MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'purchase' THEN event_ts END) AS last_purchase
FROM events
GROUP BY user_id
ORDER BY user_id;

examples.title: Share of total via a conditional sum
examples.explain_md: East's percentage of the day's revenue; the conditional `SUM` is the numerator, plain `SUM` the denominator.
examples.mysql:
SELECT sale_date,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'East' THEN revenue ELSE 0 END) / SUM(revenue), 1) AS east_pct
FROM daily_sales
WHERE sale_date <= '2024-03-05'
GROUP BY sale_date
ORDER BY sale_date;
examples.tsql:
SELECT sale_date,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'East' THEN revenue ELSE 0 END) / SUM(revenue), 1) AS east_pct
FROM daily_sales
WHERE sale_date <= '2024-03-05'
GROUP BY sale_date
ORDER BY sale_date;

sections.heading: SQL Server PIVOT (and why conditional aggregation still wins)
sections.body_md:
- `PIVOT` is SQL Server (and Oracle) sugar for conditional aggregation. **MySQL has no PIVOT keyword**: use the previous sections.
- Shape: `FROM (source subquery) AS s PIVOT (AGG(value) FOR category IN ([A], [B])) AS p`.
- The `IN` list is **hard-coded literals** (bracketed names); it cannot be a subquery.
- Select **only the three needed columns** in the source subquery; any extra column silently becomes a grouping key.
- One aggregate only, with no CASE logic; missing combinations come back as NULL.
- Interview tip: write the conditional-aggregation form (portable), then mention PIVOT as the SQL Server shortcut.

syntax.mysql: -- no PIVOT in MySQL: use SUM(CASE WHEN ...) per output column

args.name: (SELECT key, cat, val ...) AS src
args.meaning: Source rows: exactly the row key, the pivot column and the value. Extra columns become extra grouping keys.

args.name: FOR cat
args.meaning: The column whose distinct values become new columns.

args.name: IN ([A], [B])
args.meaning: The literal values to turn into columns; unlisted values are dropped.

examples.title: The same result as the first example, with PIVOT
examples.explain_md: MySQL uses conditional aggregation without ELSE (NULL for missing); SQL Server's PIVOT returns the identical grid.
examples.mysql:
SELECT sale_date,
       SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'East' THEN revenue END) AS East,
       SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'West' THEN revenue END) AS West
FROM daily_sales
WHERE sale_date <= '2024-03-05'
GROUP BY sale_date
ORDER BY sale_date;
examples.tsql:
SELECT sale_date, [East], [West]
FROM (SELECT sale_date, region, revenue
      FROM daily_sales
      WHERE sale_date <= '2024-03-05') AS src
PIVOT (SUM(revenue) FOR region IN ([East], [West])) AS p
ORDER BY sale_date;
examples.dialect_note_md: MySQL has no `PIVOT`; the MySQL query is the portable equivalent.

pitfalls_md: Forgetting the narrowing subquery and pivoting a whole table gives one row per unique combination of all other columns.
Values missing from the `IN` list vanish without an error.

sections.heading: Unpivot (columns to rows)
sections.body_md:
- **Portable**: one `SELECT` per column glued with `UNION ALL`, adding a label column. Keeps NULLs unless you filter them.
- **Lookup join**: cross join the table with a small list of labels and pick the column with `CASE`; one scan instead of N.
- **SQL Server** also has `UNPIVOT` (drops NULL values) and `CROSS APPLY (VALUES ...)`. MySQL has neither.
- Long format is what you want before grouping, charting or window functions across the former columns.

syntax.mysql:
SELECT id, 'Q1' AS label, q1 AS value FROM t
UNION ALL SELECT id, 'Q2', q2 FROM t
UNION ALL SELECT id, 'Q3', q3 FROM t;   -- ORDER BY after the last SELECT
syntax.tsql:
-- UNPIVOT
SELECT id, label, value
FROM t
UNPIVOT (value FOR label IN (q1, q2, q3)) AS u;

-- or CROSS APPLY
SELECT t.id, v.label, v.value
FROM t CROSS APPLY (VALUES ('Q1', q1), ('Q2', q2), ('Q3', q3)) AS v(label, value);

args.name: 'Q1' AS label
args.meaning: Literal that records which column the value came from.

args.name: q1 AS value
args.meaning: The wide column being turned into a row value. All value columns must share a type.

args.name: UNPIVOT (value FOR label IN (...))
args.meaning: SQL Server: `value` = new value column, `label` = new name column, list = source columns.

args.name: ORDER BY
args.meaning: Applies to the whole UNION; use output column names.

examples.title: UNION ALL unpivot
examples.explain_md: Twelve rows, one per product and quarter, including the NULL cells for Widget Q3 and Gadget Q2.

tables.name: quarterly_sales
tables.description_md: Wide table: one row per product, one column per quarter. `NULL` means no sales figure was recorded.

examples.mysql:
SELECT product, 'Q1' AS qtr, q1 AS units FROM quarterly_sales
UNION ALL
SELECT product, 'Q2', q2 FROM quarterly_sales
UNION ALL
SELECT product, 'Q3', q3 FROM quarterly_sales
UNION ALL
SELECT product, 'Q4', q4 FROM quarterly_sales
ORDER BY product, qtr;
examples.tsql:
SELECT product, 'Q1' AS qtr, q1 AS units FROM quarterly_sales
UNION ALL
SELECT product, 'Q2', q2 FROM quarterly_sales
UNION ALL
SELECT product, 'Q3', q3 FROM quarterly_sales
UNION ALL
SELECT product, 'Q4', q4 FROM quarterly_sales
ORDER BY product, qtr;

examples.title: Drop the NULL cells
examples.explain_md: Filtering `units IS NOT NULL` reproduces what SQL Server's UNPIVOT does automatically: 10 rows.

tables.name: quarterly_sales
tables.description_md: Wide table: one row per product, one column per quarter. `NULL` means no sales figure was recorded.

examples.mysql:
SELECT product, qtr, units
FROM (SELECT product, 'Q1' AS qtr, q1 AS units FROM quarterly_sales
      UNION ALL SELECT product, 'Q2', q2 FROM quarterly_sales
      UNION ALL SELECT product, 'Q3', q3 FROM quarterly_sales
      UNION ALL SELECT product, 'Q4', q4 FROM quarterly_sales) AS u
WHERE units IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY product, qtr;
examples.tsql:
SELECT product, qtr, units
FROM (SELECT product, 'Q1' AS qtr, q1 AS units FROM quarterly_sales
      UNION ALL SELECT product, 'Q2', q2 FROM quarterly_sales
      UNION ALL SELECT product, 'Q3', q3 FROM quarterly_sales
      UNION ALL SELECT product, 'Q4', q4 FROM quarterly_sales) AS u
WHERE units IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY product, qtr;

examples.title: Cross join with a label list
examples.explain_md: One scan of the wide table; the `CASE` picks the matching column for each label. Same 12 rows as the UNION ALL version.

tables.name: quarterly_sales
tables.description_md: Wide table: one row per product, one column per quarter. `NULL` means no sales figure was recorded.

examples.mysql:
SELECT s.product, k.qtr,
       CASE k.qtr WHEN 'Q1' THEN s.q1 WHEN 'Q2' THEN s.q2 WHEN 'Q3' THEN s.q3 ELSE s.q4 END AS units
FROM quarterly_sales s
CROSS JOIN (SELECT 'Q1' AS qtr UNION ALL SELECT 'Q2' UNION ALL SELECT 'Q3' UNION ALL SELECT 'Q4') AS k
ORDER BY s.product, k.qtr;
examples.tsql:
SELECT s.product, k.qtr,
       CASE k.qtr WHEN 'Q1' THEN s.q1 WHEN 'Q2' THEN s.q2 WHEN 'Q3' THEN s.q3 ELSE s.q4 END AS units
FROM quarterly_sales s
CROSS JOIN (SELECT 'Q1' AS qtr UNION ALL SELECT 'Q2' UNION ALL SELECT 'Q3' UNION ALL SELECT 'Q4') AS k
ORDER BY s.product, k.qtr;

examples.title: Why long format helps: total per quarter
examples.explain_md: After unpivoting, a normal GROUP BY totals each quarter (SUM skips the NULLs).

tables.name: quarterly_sales
tables.description_md: Wide table: one row per product, one column per quarter. `NULL` means no sales figure was recorded.

examples.mysql:
SELECT qtr, SUM(units) AS total_units
FROM (SELECT 'Q1' AS qtr, q1 AS units FROM quarterly_sales
      UNION ALL SELECT 'Q2', q2 FROM quarterly_sales
      UNION ALL SELECT 'Q3', q3 FROM quarterly_sales
      UNION ALL SELECT 'Q4', q4 FROM quarterly_sales) AS u
GROUP BY qtr
ORDER BY qtr;
examples.tsql:
SELECT qtr, SUM(units) AS total_units
FROM (SELECT 'Q1' AS qtr, q1 AS units FROM quarterly_sales
      UNION ALL SELECT 'Q2', q2 FROM quarterly_sales
      UNION ALL SELECT 'Q3', q3 FROM quarterly_sales
      UNION ALL SELECT 'Q4', q4 FROM quarterly_sales) AS u
GROUP BY qtr
ORDER BY qtr;

pitfalls_md: `UNION` (without ALL) would also de-duplicate identical rows and sort: almost never what you want here.
UNPIVOT skips NULL cells; `UNION ALL` keeps them. Say which you want.

sections.heading: Dynamic columns
sections.body_md:
- SQL needs the output column list at **parse time**, so a pivot over unknown values cannot be a single static query.
- Options: (1) pivot in the application or BI tool, (2) return **long format** and let the client reshape, (3) generate the SQL text and run it as dynamic SQL.
- Dynamic SQL recipe: build the `CASE` list from `SELECT DISTINCT`, concatenate it into the full statement, execute it.
  - MySQL: `GROUP_CONCAT` -> `SET @sql = ...; PREPARE s FROM @sql; EXECUTE s;`
  - SQL Server: `STRING_AGG` (2017+) or `STUFF(... FOR XML PATH)` -> `EXEC sp_executesql @sql;`
- Raise `group_concat_max_len` (default 1024) in MySQL if the generated list is long. Quote identifiers (`QUOTENAME` in SQL Server) to avoid injection.

syntax.tsql:
DECLARE @sql NVARCHAR(MAX) = N'SELECT sale_date, ' + @cols + N' FROM daily_sales GROUP BY sale_date';
EXEC sp_executesql @sql;

args.name: @cols
args.meaning: The generated column list from the query above.

args.name: PREPARE / EXECUTE
args.meaning: MySQL's dynamic SQL; inside stored routines or the client session.

args.name: sp_executesql
args.meaning: SQL Server's parameter-safe dynamic SQL executor.

examples.title: Generate the pivot column list from the data
examples.explain_md: Builds the `SUM(CASE ...)` fragments for every distinct region; this string is what you would splice into the final SELECT before executing it.
examples.dialect_note_md: MySQL: `GROUP_CONCAT(expr ORDER BY ... SEPARATOR ...)`. SQL Server 2017+: `STRING_AGG(..., sep) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ...)`; de-duplicate in a subquery first.

rows: SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'East' THEN revenue END) AS East, SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'West' THEN revenue END) AS West

pitfalls_md: Dynamic SQL built from data values is an injection risk: whitelist or quote identifiers.
Interview answer: 'column list must be known at parse time, so I would reshape downstream or generate the SQL'.
